analysis:
All three changed files are offline CI regression tests (scripts/test-ci-component-paths.py, scripts/test-cluster-test-plan.py, scripts/test-provider-ci-workflow.py). They touch no provider runtime, coordinator protocol, key custody, attestation or authorization code, so no threat-model asset (A-001..A-019) or trust boundary (TB-002/003/007/009/011/012/013) has changed behavior in this PR.

The tests now pin new CI workflow behavior that is defined in files I did not see:
- A shared .git cache is restored with a cold-checkout fallback. Only the cached checkout may set continue-on-error; the cold retry may not.
- Checkouts use persist-credentials: false, and the test comment says a persisted token would be saved with .git/config. This is a sound credential-leak control.
- Cache saves are limited to pushes to master and dev (SAVE_CACHES), so pull requests cannot poison caches; the composite action is guarded the same way by inputs.save-caches.
- Sparse checkout excludes only docs/reports gz archives and landing mp4 files.
- The tests assert no secrets., environment, id-token or repository: in ci.yml, provider-release-cache.yml and component-changes.yml.
- The provider-test-gate truth table still requires success for selected lanes and skipped for unselected lanes.

Relaxing assertNotIn continue-on-error to exclude the cached checkout step is a narrow, intentional test change. without_cached_checkout removes only the step with id checkout, and the tests separately assert that the fallback steps are fail-closed.

Residual question: the workflow YAML (.github/workflows/ci.yml, the composite action) is outside this batch. Whether the real workflow matches these assertions, and whether restoring a .git cache saved from master and used in pull-request jobs is a poisoning vector (a stale or hostile .git state), cannot be confirmed here. The cache is saved only from push events to trusted branches, which mitigates this. The next pass should check that the workflow matches the assertions. No findings.
